lines: Your vowels are from Thessaloniki, Sophia. I'd stake my register on it, so tell me which part.
Ano Poli, up by the walls. My mother taught literature at the school there.
Then you walked past my father's funeral home every day of your childhood. I'd have nodded to you on the stairs.
The one on the hill with the heavy door? I was terrified of that door until I was twelve.
Stelios, your wife's name is Despina, isn't it? At the old library?
It is, and she stamped every book in that building herself.
She stamped mine, every Saturday for six years. She let me take four when the rule was three.
That sounds exactly like her. She always said the rules were for people who didn't read, and I'd like her to know you remember.
I keep the register in Greek as well as Common. Would you check my spelling? The dead deserve their accents in the right place.
I'd be honoured. I'll also correct your handwriting, I'm afraid, it's a funeral director's scrawl.
Funeral directors write beautifully, Sophia, we just do it in a hurry.
My father had started losing people, before all this. He still knew me, mostly, and I hold on to the mostly.
I've sat with a great many families holding on to a mostly. It isn't a small thing to hold, and some days it's the whole of it.
Thank you. You put that exactly right, and I've listened to the best speakers in Europe.
Nineteen years of practice, and a city that taught us both to talk slowly.
Suit check, Taras. I know you've done it, and I'm doing it anyway.
Every morning, and you've never once found anything wrong.
That's how you know it's working.
Kashtan, sit, the man's doing his job. He'll check you next, and you'll like it.
My tourists used to ask if Chernobyl could happen again, Wes. I'd tell them only if people stop being careful.
Hanford had folks saying it'll be fine for fifty years. We spent twenty cleaning up after them.
So it's the same job, you and me, from two ends. Somebody makes the mess, and we count the heads.
Copy that, it's the same job.
The mule's started following Kashtan around when I'm on shift.
Kashtan's very proud of it. He's never had a mule before.
Me neither, to be fair. I didn't ask for this one.
Nobody asks for the good things here, Wes. They just turn up and eat your apples.
My father was a liquidator in 1986. He went in so the rest of us wouldn't have to.
My dad fitted pipe at Hanford his whole life. He never said much about what was in them.
Then we both grew up next to something nobody would talk about. Maybe that's why we keep the fence.
Could be, Taras. Somebody's got to stand at it who knows what's on the other side.
You cook, my friend? I can smell it on you, onion and paprika.
I don't cook, I make beans. And you smell like somebody who burns meat and calls it a skill.
Burns, you say? Che, I ran a grill for twelve years.
Then you've been burning things for twelve years, bre, and well done.
I tried your asado last night, Argentine. It needed salt.
It needed nothing! You put salt on everything, your tongue is broken.
My tongue fed forty regulars every night in Novi Sad, and none of them complained.
Because they were afraid of you, che! I've seen your face.
Okay, I'll say it once, and if you tell anybody I'll deny it. Your beans are good, Vuk.
Just good, is it? They're the best beans in Serbia.
They're good, that's all. Mine would be better, if I made beans, which I don't, because I've got standards.
Ha, so eat another bowl and say that again, bre.
Your meat and my beans, on the same night, at one fire. People would come from three zones.
A cook-off, my friend? You'd lose, and you'd lose in front of everybody.
Not a cook-off. One table, both of us at it, and nobody leaves hungry.
Now that, che, I would come to. I might even sit down at it.
My grandmother always said people who argue about food are the only honest ones, Vuk.
Uncle Dragan would have thrown you out of his kitchen for touching his pot, and then fed you.
That's the same thing, my friend. That's exactly the same thing.
Allora, a Cuban! I had a Cuban regular once who drank mojitos at seven in the morning, and I never judged him.
Perfect, then I'll do the conversation for both of us, dai.
That's what I was afraid of.
You know what you need, Osvaldo? A bar with a little stage, and a band on a Thursday.
Every bar needs music! I'd keep a corner for you, and I wouldn't talk through it, I promise.
You'd talk through it, asere. You'd talk through your own funeral.
You stopped talking for a whole minute in that fight, and I noticed.
I was concentrating! It happens, rarely, but it happens.
Don't do it again. It was strange, and I didn't like it.
Mamma mia, he likes my talking! I knew it, I always know.
I said I didn't like the quiet, asere, and that's different.
I rate everything out of ten, you know that. Your fire's a nine, Osvaldo.
Nobody gets a ten. Not my coffee, not my wife's cooking, not even me.
Then I'll take the nine. It's better than the hotel manager ever gave me.
You talk so nobody hears what you don't say, Gianluca. I know, because I keep quiet for the same reason.
You're a dangerous man, you know that? Sitting there quietly, noticing everything.
Sit with me a while. You don't have to say it, I just want you to know I heard it.
Your accent's Achrafieh, habibi. Don't tell me, near the sea, below Sassine?
Two streets from the clinic on the hill, the one by the church. Ten years drawing blood there.
I've driven up that hill a thousand times with the siren on! I probably brought you half your patients.
Then you're the reason my Tuesdays were so busy. I always wondered who to blame.
You heal with fel, Ziad, and I heal with blood. Our mothers would want a word with both of us.
Mine would ask if it's working. It's working, so she'd make coffee and stop asking.
Mine would make coffee too, and then ask anyway, all afternoon.
That's an Achrafieh mother. They never stop asking, and they're always right.
You're slower than me and you're still always on time, Elie. How do you manage it?
I talk the whole way through. The patient forgets to panic, and when nobody panics, nothing goes wrong.
I just run, faster than the panic, every time.
And who catches you when you trip, habibi?
The port, Ziad. I was at the clinic that day, and people came in for hours, cut by the glass, and I kept thinking about whoever was out there choosing.
That was us, me and three vans. I don't talk about it.
You don't have to. I just wanted you to know somebody at the other end was catching them.
Thank you, habibi. I always wondered if anyone was.
